title: Was I supposed to be sympathetic to Travis in Paris, Texas?

commenti.body: I think the reason people like Paris, Texas is because it doesn't try to sway you one way or another, it just is. People make decisions in their lives for one reason or another and its mostly a mystery to those around them. You spend 147 minutes with this guy and you don't know anything more about him at the end than when you started.

I was going to say something similar but you hit the nail on the head. I think it’s one of those movies where you can both sympathize with someone and also not sympathize with them. Humans aren’t black and white and neither is he. He just exists.
[removed]

You can be sympathetic towards someone who makes terrible choices. I don’t find that difficult to do. We’re all flawed and terrible. None of us will pass the scales of Anubis. 

The idea that movie characters somehow have to be paragons of virtue to deserve being protagonists, and to deserve examination and sympathy, is a very recent one, and highly annoying.

I've seen movies where the protagonist is a bad or morally ambiguous person and enjoyed them very much. But I feel that in this case the film very much tries to sway you into one direction. At the end Jane and Hunter are reunited, they fall into each other's arms, they're happy. Travis drives away into the sunset. He finally fixed his mistakes. That's the interpretation I feel the film is swaying me towards.
Sorry I'm not sympathetic towards old guys preying on teenagers and kidnapping children
Must be nice.

I see it differently though, I feel like Travis thinks he's fixed his mistakes but actually just made things worse really. 

He's ruined the life of his brother and wife by taking away the child who was basically their son at this point and given him to Jane who is a sex worker with no support from anybody else. She is going to struggle raising a child on her own which she knew and is why she left Hunter with the brother.

Ironically everybody would have been better off if Ttavis had just never came back.
No

I don't understand the need to like a character to empathize with him, and the idea that characters have to be good in order for it to be ok to sympathize with them. If you treat movies this way, then why even watch them? What's the point in making complex emotional narratives? Are we really considering ourselves more moral because we dislike "bad" characters in movies?

Totally agree, I think the movie presents Travis as "authentic" while Walt and Anne are phony because they live in LA and Walt works in advertising. Travis is supposed to be this heroic figure for rescuing his son from this hellhole. Also, we are supposed to see Travis as noble for abandoning his son again at the end of the movie.

I think it’s not about sympathy but empathy. You spend an hour and a half walking in a guy’s shoes, do you feel he has humanity you can relate to? 

I watch movies about criminals, killers, and I don’t think they’re right. But I experience the world through their eyes for a while. I think that’s what cinema is all about.
You're right, but at the same time this is Harry Dean Stanton we're talking about. We know nothing in the literal sense, but just one look into his eyes and in another sense we know everything.

I haven’t seen the movie in a long time but I don’t think it was the filmmakers intention for you to have sympathy for Travis. That’s why this movie is still talked about quite a bit still after so many years. Much of the movie is left to the viewer to make up their own mind. A more recent movie that I felt was like this was Hell or High Water.
[removed]

It is a film about the frailty of the human psyche and we get to know several characters that struggle through life. For me, an anchor point also was Hunter and how he deserves to break the cycle of unhappiness and trauma. 
Both his parents are full of regret and are damaged and have lived years full of shame. They have carried a lot of pain, depression and self hatred for years. They know they should have been there for their son but could not deal with their own hurt and their own struggles. 

And they get a second chance to build some kind of a relationship and there is hope for Hunter to build some sort of bond to both his parents in the future. There is no repairing what was lost, but there is hope for forgiveness and healing to a point. A happy family is not in the cards, the film is honest in that regard, but maybe there is a chance for them to be able to forgive themselves and be a part of Hunters life, even if it is not in a life together, there is hope that he will maybe not resent them. 

The film is not idealizing its main characters, it lays bare the frailty of our lives, shows us people who break down over life’s struggles. And it gives them a chance to start healing their hurts. And I love it for that.

This is one of the many reasons I love this film. I find Agnes Varda’s Vagabond enthralling in a similar way. Notable parallels between the two protagonists too, for example with ones first appearance being “materialised” in the desert, and the others emergence from the ocean.

Really not sure how you can watch the movie and look at Travis as “heroic.” It’s not a movie of heroes, and his way of life is not glamorized at all, it’s deeply sad. He’s a guy who can’t take life straight despite longing for connection. He mostly ends up hurting everyone around him, and his one true act of kindness at the end is to literally remove himself from the picture once more.

I think the point of the way of the movie is structured is that we, the audience, are totally ignorant as to who this character is beyond a single albeit defining trait, his new “nomadism”. It tracks why most people’s first watch elicits a sympathetic reaction, Harry Dean Stanton adopts this lost puppy like appearance. 

The catharsis of the film lies in the fact that, as the film unfolds, we start to see him as a real human being. A human being with baggage. A TON of it. 

I don’t think the film explicitly wants you to feel any particular way about the situation, but I do think the unambiguous part is that it asks whether or not Travis can successfully repair a situation which he messed up so badly, largely by being a terrible person. Is he still a terrible person for employing a correct solution too late? Is he still ultimately selfish with more altruistic methods? Will things improve based on his messy actions? I think the beauty of the film comes with those questions that we simply can never know the answer to, in real life or in the case of this film.
The film doesn’t ask you to be sympathetic to Travis. The fact that you can’t consider the character on any other level is a sign that your media literacy is very low.

I have no problem watching unsympathetic people but I was rather annoyed with Travis' decision to take the boy back to his mother. I did feel like the movie wanted me to feel like that is a good thing but I could be misinterpretating it. Still enjoyed it overall, especially the cinematography.

I've pretty much soured on cinema's insistence on having us focus with such absorption, on toxic masculinity or, if for some reason you don't like the term assholes. This came from an era where we were fascinated with Taxi Driver and Raging Bull and the Shining and on and on. They're great films, obviously, but they show what a fucked up culture we have where these protagonists are worthy of our attention instead of, say, the people they hurt.
Not true . You do know more , a lot more I’d say .
[removed]

I’ve been saying this lately. Like why are four out of every five “great films” about some toxicly masculine antihero. And I love a lot of these movies by the way (Taxi Driver for example), but can we just write about something else. It’s been like a hundred years, from Citizen Cane to Wolf of Wall Street, the same old shit. Men with a mad desire for potency that ultimately destroys them and/or the people around them but goddammit at least they kept their balls.

Yes. Being sympathetic to someone doesn’t mean you have to think they’re a good person. He does a lot of awful things, and wants to make up for them. Even while making up for them, he does bad things. The movie is about generational trauma, regret. Travis talking about his parents, the scenes in the club, even his brother and his wife talking about the past. You don’t have to root for people to have empathy towards them and their pain

I never really thought of his actions as being objectively right or wrong. The movie basically puts you into his head space, and you feel what he feels: at times confused, then determined, and ultimately assured that you made the best decision. I agree the movie paints him as a tragic hero, but it’s a film that’s very subjective in its main character’s viewpoint. Just an emotionally destroyed man who did what he thought was best.
[removed]

I don’t hear OP at all saying he can’t abide a bad character—I hear him saying there’s something about this character that is infuriating. And I agree, although I only saw it once 4 decades ago, so my judgement is provisional.

I loved Walter White but hated Tony Montana. Loved Michael Corleone but hated Colonel Kurtz. Loved all 3 leads in Rebel Without a Cause but hated all 3 in Giant. Loved the protagonist of Light Sleeper but hated the one in First Reformed.

Sometimes a writer, director and actor win me over and sometimes they make me resent them for trying. It’s not about good and evil or likable or not.
I agree with you and I’d like to add that I’m a fan and admirer of Ry Cooder, but I found his much-praised score for this film excruciating.
Except all his comments come across like he can’t abide a bad character

I agree he focuses a lot on bad stuff Travis does, but there’s at least one comment where he says there are plenty of other bad or unlikeable characters he has gotten something out of watching.

My point (and I believe it’s OP’s as well) is that sometimes it feels like the director is determined to make you sympathize with a character, and sometimes that just makes you resent the character *and* the director. I get that most people in this sub don’t feel that way about Paris, TX. But surely there’s some other film you feel that way about?

The film could've used one final shot a la The Graduate where you just see the fear or regret on the mother's face to indicate a layer of uncertainty about the future. Because yeah the ending feels a bit too neat compared with the nuanced mess that came before, like we *assume* she's grown as a person but aren't really given any nailed on proof of it. The film is perfect otherwise imo, just the ending keeps it a 4.5 instead of a 5 for me personally. But some might argue that Travis leaving again inherently indicates that the cycles of failure will continue, idk.
[removed]

OP isn't doing the best at making or defending their point but I've got to agree that the movie does romanticize Travis' situation and that it's pretty obnoxious at times. Most people who disagree with OP are trying to make this point that the movie doesn't attempt to sway the audience one way or the other but that's definitely not what it felt like to me, either. Comments are also attacking OP for hating a movie that chooses to focus on a shit person, and I don't know if that's really their issue, but I think what is an issue is that the movie doesn't seem to realize how shit of a person Travis is.

I don't know, it's been a while since I watched this one, but I also came away from it with a bad taste in my mouth. Felt like a movie made by a man during a time when the world gave men way more free passes. Maybe the problem is that it hasn't aged well.
i agree, i don't hear really hear people talk about this in reviews of the movie. i liked this film as a teenager but the whole 50 year old with a 17 year old certainly sours the film for me.

I am a fan of the movie, it is extremely well shot and very emotionally moving, but I also have to agree that the movie does seem to put a positive spin on Travis’s kidnapping of the child from his adoptive parents and returning him to his biological mother. I thought the movie presented it as a redemptive act that atones for his prior conduct and it doesn’t seem to care about the impact on the adoptive parents, who if I remember correctly don’t have any screen time at all after the kidnapping happened. 

I look past it because the movie is so well made, but that part did strike me the wrong way and leaves a bit of a bad taste in the mouth if you think about it too much.

And we get downvoted for saying so. There's something fucked up about American and Hollywood culture, infantile, violent, unable or not interested in growing out of childish masculine rage, and in part it's because a lot of film makers and cinephiles simply admire that shit.

Exactly, sometimes you can watch a movie with a reprehensible character and it will be interesting because it has something to say, other times if it doesn’t have anything to add it’s just a story where you’re watching someone be awful for no reason. There has to be a value to a movie to make watching a bad character worth it
[removed]

I think at the end Travis’ arc is complete.  He has made peace with himself.

The actual reality of everyone’s life remains complicated, but what else is new?
I always kinda figured she called Dean Stockwell and he came to pick up the kid

I think if you're not sympathetic, then you simply don't understand the complexities and complications of life. It's messy and rough, and it's never what you want, but in the end, it all works itself out some way. He's a man who is aware of what he's done wrong in life and doesn't know how to make it right. He's lost. In the end he knows the right thing is reuniting his child with his mother and stepping away knowing how toxic he is to them. Is he a good guy? No. Is he a bad guy? No. Is he complicated? Isn't everything?  
  
You just made me rewatch this film for the first time in a long time... there are only a handful of movies that make me cry, and this is one.

When I watched the movie, I thought the same as you about Travis right afterward. About the film overall, I thought, "pretty, but I don't get the hype", I didn't find it very deep, I wasn't really moved much. But I'm telling you, this movie just sticks with you. Days, weeks went by, and at some point I just found it'd dug a little nest in my heart. 

Think about the score, the visuals. Think about the tension during those conversation scenes. They werent sad, to me, per se, I wasn't feeling much for Travis, mostly I felt bad for Jane and thought Travis was pretty fucked up. But there was a matter-of-factness to the story, to the events, that made even what I considered a pretty inconsequential, anticlimactic resolution, oddly satisfying. Not satisfying in the classical way, but in the way that it mimics life. People do bad shit. And they make weird choices. And they wander, and stumble. They leave you with more questions than answers. That's a truth in itself, and it suffices to wrap up an otherwise pretty barren story. You're pretty much just being moved through a fairly eventless roadtrip, given a pretty modest reveal to an otherwise only moderately compelling mystery, and then the two split off and go their own ways. We don't know what happens to Travis, we can assume he maybe is okay due to having family, but they're gonna feel weird about the situation. Jane, on its face, seems pretty screwed, but she got by okay thus far. They both might be headed to ruin, or they may make decent new lives for themselves. That's just how it is.

The act of reuniting mother and son \*is\* honourable, in theory. But that wasn't his original goal, and it comes at the cost of a lot of things, including for his brother and sister-in-law. The fact that the movie allows the scenes between father and son to be funny and moving doesn't negate that there is darkness and terrible sadness running under it all. That the movie does both things at once is what makes it special.

It's because the toxic masculine has been the driving force behind everything that embodies America, and frankly, much of the world. It's one of the THE central problems of humanity and society, and is thus fertile and important ground for films to cover, and when they do it well, it is often deeply felt.
By this logic you should also sour on people being killed in movies

I agree with parts of OP's comments and the critics. I view this as a great movie, but it does leave a bad taste. I don't believe anyone has mentioned one major reason for this, which is less the so-called kidnapping than the fact that Jane is a sex worker, which essentially means that she becomes Travis's demented fantasy of her, thus proving Travis "right" is retrospect. In this light he is all the more heroic for now accepting her. At the same time part of what makes this great is that the film is interested in the way fantasy in film works, evident through the interview scene in the sex booth and then Travis's imitation of the Searchers.

This fantastic film is exceptional in that it involves ambivalence something almost unseen in commercial movies. The movie transcends the idea of good & evil individuals that most popular films force upon their audience. It actively involves its audience as autonomous thinkers instead of implying their stupidity. The movie requires you to watch it differently and rid yourself of thinking in these comforting pluralistic categories („shit person“) even if that makes it much more uncomfortable.

That's exactly my point. I have no issues with unlikable protagonists. I loved Red Rocket, I loved Breaking Bad. But the film definitely tries to sway you one way. And with Jane saying that she kept thinking about Travis, maybe loving him, with no indication that Travis had been predatory towards her seems a bit too much like an old man's fantasy about fucking teenagers that was much more accepted 40 years ago than today

Yes! Op seems juvenile in their assessment of life and the amount of control we have on things. 
Moral superiority is a nasty thing.
[removed]

Mm I think it's that some characters are just so disgusting that you can't believe that the story is trying to make you empathize with them. I haven't watched this movie but from what op has said yeah, I also wouldn't be able to empathize or look for the good things or think that it's a Grey character or tolerate a predator. They just disgust me and make me want not to watch a movie that tries to make me like them or not feel disgusted by them lol, probably op comes from a similar place

I’ll go out on my limb here and say, “No. I don’t believe you were supposed to relate in any way to Travis.”

My interpretation of the film is that we’re intended to place ourselves in the shoes of Travis’s many victims, never his. We *see* his shoes for 145 minutes, and he’s not a complicated character. He’s shallow and selfish and wildly immature. Wenders makes him very human, but to me it felt like he went to great lengths to communicate just how awful and deluded he was. His own catharsis was just as hollow and destructive as everything else in his life. The power in the story is with those lives disrupted by his bullshit. 

To this point, I still think the two most powerful scenes that exist as a juxtaposition are (1) when Travis’s son is forced to be a therapist (with Travis literally laying on a couch and unloading his burdens) and (2) when the son is reunited with the mom and all he can muster is, “Your hair…it’s wet.” Neither scene is about Travis at all — he’s just the shitty catalyst. But we see a child, first forced to be mature beyond his years because his dad is a fuck, who’s slick facade absolutely shatters when faced with such an overwhelming, beautiful, painful, uncertain moment. 

And every other powerful moment, in my opinion, is likewise only powerful because of the victims’ perspectives. We barely see the adoptive parents, yet I felt like I was the one waiting by the phone for an update on my child’s safety. 

I love the film. But if I thought Wenders was trying to make Travis into a relatable character, I’d call the whole thing a massive failure.
I'm not sure Jane would have been better off, but the rest maybe
OK, so stick to Marvel from now on
Maybe the movie has aged well but the world's gotten worse.

I give the filmmaker enough credit to assume that us not seeing the adoptive parents anymore after that was intentional. Travis doesn't seem to care about them and children have very short memories, you take them on a road trip and the world changes for them.

I don't think it's fair to say that Travis 'kidnaps' Hunter. Hunter is given the choice whether he wants to stay with Walt and Anne or to leave and try and find Jane. Travis tells him that he may not see Walt and Anne for a long time, but also tells him that they can turn back any time he wants. Hunter gets to make the choice, but also has to face the consequences of his decision (phoning Anne to tell her what they've done and hearing the sadness in her voice).

Giving a small child this kind of agency over their life and care is a radical act, and the heart of the movie for me. I don't disagree that Travis comes across as unlikeable in many ways (his revulsion at Jane's work is pretty appalling even before we find out the background), and I wish Jane's side of the story was more fleshed out, but readings that strip away Hunter's agency miss the point IMO.

Also remember that both Walt and Anne facilitate Travis taking Hunter to find Jane, even though they must have an idea what he is planning and that it will break their hearts.

I don’t get the whole movie. The cinematography is beautiful but the story and the characters don’t really engage. I feel like a lot of people say it’s one of their favorite movies because it sounds cool to say that.

The harsh truth is that every predator and bad person that ever lived has a lot in common with most people, yourself included. In our humanity we all share so many characteristics. Even those who make the most reprehensible choices known to man possess some noble qualities, or did sometime in their life, or will again in the future. We cannot just shove them under the rug and pretend they do not exist, or that we do not share parts of our own experience with them.

They just don't deserve empathy,there are some stuff that make ppl irredeemable , sure they might have some decent qualities but the bad far outweighs the good, ofc we can do that, don't we throw them in jail and let them rot?  Ig some countries don't, they should.

I might offer that feeling empathy is compartmental, and sometimes involuntary. For example, we can witness a man who has done horrible things experience a tender moment with his mother. We can empathize with him in that moment. It is a shared human experience. We do not look at the whole man, but on the moment alone, and we feel empathy on impulse, without reflection on his entire catalogue of life choices which may be overwhelmingly grotesque. But we understand tenderness with our own mothers, and even in that horrible man there is or once was a little child lost and scared in the world. There are large parts of him that we cannot understand, and abhor, but we can still emphasize even with our worst enemy. We must admit of the good even in the most evil, or we become blind to ourselves.
Mm I can see that, the impulse thing does happen sometimes to me but is a rather fleeting feeling you know? It goes away kinda quickly once I remember what I'm looking at

I understand that completely. As a philosophical exercise it may sometime be interesting to lean into that empathetic feeling, even when the character on film is repulsive to you. It could shed some light on your own personhood and what it means to be a flawed human being in this complicated world.

I completely agree. Some of my absolute favorite films are about that stuff. Paul Thomas Anderson’s The Master for example (and by the way, don’t get me wrong, I love Paris, Texas). But it’s not uncommon that I see in certain films something that feels like admiration for these men. As if there’s something noble or admirable in their pursuit of power and efficacy at all cost. They burn up gloriously in the sun and whatnot. And I think it’s less that I find that problematic and more that I just find it boring. Idk, I’m worried I’m coming off as overly moralistic in my evaluation of art, but I don’t mean to be. I want to say something about Simone Weil’s idea that beauty is all about where we put our attention, but I’m not sure if I have the right words at the moment.
